lesson.title: Audit an AI tool
lesson.subtitle: Test it on work like your pupils’ before you trust it

video.title: Audit an AI tool
video.format_note: Animated explainer, 16:9, flat Darsi colours on paper-grey backgrounds, one recurring teacher character. Narration in the lesson language; captions as separate files, never burned in.
cast: Dr Farah Rahman — teacher educator, Bangladesh (main character)
Mr Okafor — Grade 8 science teacher, Nigeria (cameo)
Narrator — the Darsi voice (warm, peer to peer)

scenes.visual: A district office meeting room. A supplier’s brochure on the table shows a phone with a microphone icon and a big “95% accurate” badge. Dr Farah picks it up, looks at the badge, then at the camera: one eyebrow raised.
scenes.animation: Brochure slides in; the badge pops (≤ 200 ms). Quick push-in on Farah’s face.
scenes.narration: A supplier told our district their reading app is ninety-five per cent accurate. My first question was: accurate for whom?

scenes.visual: Paper-grey card. The Darsi mark pops in, then the course name, the lesson title and a yellow ‘AI’ track chip with the spark icon.
scenes.animation: Mark scales 0→100% with a small overshoot (≤ 200 ms); title slides up.
scenes.narration: Today: audit an AI tool before your school trusts it.

scenes.visual: A phone listens to a child reading aloud; each word gets a small tick or cross. A bar chart draws itself: errors overall, for city pupils and for village pupils. The village bar is six times taller.
scenes.animation: Ticks pop word by word; bars grow left to right (1.5 s).
scenes.on_screen_text: One number can hide a group
scenes.narration: The app listens to children reading aloud and marks each word. But ninety-five per cent is an average. Tested mostly on city children, it can fail village children and still score ninety-five. Voice tools often struggle with accents rare in their training.

scenes.visual: Four numbered steps build down a clipboard: choose the groups, collect samples, mark them twice (a teacher and the tool), count both kinds of error for each group.
scenes.animation: Each step slides in as it is said; a tally mark appears in each group’s column at the end.
scenes.narration: So plan a small audit. Choose the groups to compare: girls and boys, town and village, home language. Collect about twenty real samples from each group. A teacher marks them, and so does the tool. Then count its errors for each group: right answers marked wrong, and mistakes missed.

scenes.visual: Clean white card with the AI track chip. Four cards: a planned test, work like your pupils’, errors group by group, look for big gaps.
scenes.animation: Cards appear one by one, 300 ms apart.
scenes.narration: An AI audit is a planned test on work like your pupils’, comparing errors group by group. Twenty samples is small, so look for big gaps, not tiny ones.

scenes.visual: A farmer in a green field holds a seed packet showing a huge harvest. She sows one short test row beside her usual crop. Weeks later, she compares the two rows.
scenes.animation: Packet pops; the test row sprouts in a quick time-lapse (1.5 s).
scenes.narration: It’s like new seed. The packet promises a great harvest, grown somewhere else. A farmer sows one test row first, beside her usual crop. Your pupils are your soil.

scenes.visual: Mr Okafor pops in holding the “95% accurate” brochure, head tilted. Three answer cards drop in below him.
scenes.animation: Character slides in from the side; answer cards drop in with a small bounce.
scenes.narration: Quick check! A tool is ninety-five per cent accurate overall. What should you check next?

scenes.visual: The card ‘Its errors for each group’ gets a blue check badge. Split screen: on the left, one big number hides a red bar behind it; on the right, the numbers per group, the village bar in red.
scenes.animation: Check badge pops (150 ms); the big number slides aside to show the bars.
scenes.narration: Its errors for each group. A bigger test still gives one average, and that’s where a failing group hides. Ask for results per group, and if nobody has them, make them yourself.

scenes.visual: Dr Farah at a desk with a short checklist on a clipboard. Five questions tick in one by one: data and languages, testing, recordings, offline use, cost.
scenes.animation: Each question slides in as it is said.
scenes.narration: Before any pilot, ask the supplier. Whose data trained it, in which languages? Who was it tested on, with what results per group? Where do pupils’ recordings go? Does it work offline, on cheap phones? And what will it cost after the free year?

scenes.visual: Three signposts: Adopt (blue check), Pilot (a flask: one class, one term), Refuse (red cross). Under them, a teacher looks over the tool’s results.
scenes.animation: Signposts pop in one by one; the teacher slides in last.
scenes.narration: Then decide from the evidence. Adopt it when errors are low for every group. Pilot it in one class for a term when the evidence is mixed. Refuse it when a group fails or the supplier won’t answer. Either way, a teacher checks its decisions, and pupils can ask for a second look.

scenes.visual: A phone screen with the Bias in data lab: a slider for training photos from the cloudy hills, and bars for the errors. At the start, the overall bar is tiny and the ‘sick leaves missed in the hills’ bar is long.
scenes.animation: Bars grow (1 s); the slider moves right and the long bar shrinks.
scenes.on_screen_text: App lab: audit a leaf spotter
scenes.narration: In the app, you’ll audit a leaf-disease spotter trained mostly on sunny-valley photos. Overall, it’s wrong only three times in a hundred. But in the cloudy hills, it misses one sick leaf in three. Add hill photos to its training, and watch the gap close.

scenes.visual: Dr Farah holds the audit sheet: the village column full of red marks. Three answer cards appear beside her.
scenes.animation: Cards bounce in one by one.
scenes.narration: Your turn. Our audit: the app wrongly marks village readers six times as often, and the supplier hides its training data. Adopt, pilot or refuse?

scenes.visual: The ‘Refuse it, for now’ card gets the check badge, then the screen resolves into the four habits of an audit.
scenes.animation: Points tick in, 250 ms apart; the takeaway bar slides up.
scenes.narration: Refuse it, for now: a group fails, and the supplier won’t answer. Remember: test on work like your pupils’, count errors per group, ask hard questions, and decide from evidence.

scenes.visual: A classroom. Pupils take turns reading the same sentence into one phone; a pupil keeps a tally table on the board, one column per speaker and language. Dr Farah smiles beside the board.
scenes.animation: Tally marks appear on the board one by one.
scenes.narration: Try it in class tomorrow: “Test the tester”. Pupils take turns reading one sentence into voice typing, in their own voices and languages. On the board, they count its mistakes for each speaker, and discuss where it fails.

checkpoints.prompt: A tool is 95% accurate overall. What should you check next?

options.text: Its score on a bigger test

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — an overall score is an average, and it can hide one group’s failures. Check the errors group by group.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a bigger test still gives one average. Check the errors for each group of pupils.

checkpoints.prompt: The app fails village readers, and the supplier won’t share its data. Adopt, pilot or refuse?

options.text: Adopt — the overall score is high

checkpoints.feedback_correct: Correct — a group fails and the supplier won’t answer. Refuse for now, and say what evidence would change your mind.
checkpoints.feedback_wrong: Not quite — a pilot is for mixed evidence. Here a group clearly fails and the supplier won’t answer, so refuse for now.
